title: Dosage Calculation Challenge
description: Work one problem at a time. Use dimensional analysis, show your work if it helps, then check your answer.
roundingRules: Weight in kg: round to the nearest tenth.
Volume greater than 1 mL: round to the nearest tenth.
Volume less than 1 mL: round to the nearest hundredth.
Gravity drip (gtt/min): round to the nearest whole number.
Electronic pump (mL/hr): round to the nearest whole number.
BSA (m²): round to the nearest hundredth before calculating the dose.
Always follow a question's own rounding instruction when it gives one.

categories.name: IV Flow Rates – Manual Gravity Drip

questions.stem: A client weighs 200 lb. What is the weight in kg?

steps.explain: Round weight in kg to the nearest tenth.

questions.explanation: Divide the weight in pounds by 2.2.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: A client weighs 143 lb. What is the weight in kg?
questions.explanation: Divide the weight in pounds by 2.2. The answer comes out even.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: The order is digoxin 0.25 mg. How many mcg is this?

steps.explain: Moving from a larger unit (mg) to a smaller one (mcg): multiply by 1,000.

questions.explanation: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg, so 0.25 mg = 250 mcg.
mistakes: Dividing by 1,000 instead of multiplying (0.00025 mcg).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A client is ordered 1,500 mg of a medication. How many grams is this?

steps.explain: Moving from a smaller unit (mg) to a larger one (g): divide by 1,000.

questions.explanation: 1 g = 1,000 mg, so 1,500 mg = 1.5 g. Write it as 1.5 g, never 1.50 g (no trailing zero).
mistakes: Writing a trailing zero (1.50 g), which can be misread as 150.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: For intake and output, a client drank 6 oz of juice and 2 tbsp of broth. What is the total oral intake in mL? (1 oz = 30 mL, 1 tbsp = 15 mL)
questions.explanation: 6 oz is 180 mL and 2 tbsp is 30 mL, for 210 mL total.
mistakes: Using 5 mL per tbsp (that is a teaspoon).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A client's temperature is 102.2 °F. What is it in °C? Round to the nearest tenth.
questions.explanation: Subtract 32, then divide by 1.8: 102.2 °F = 39.0 °C.
mistakes: Dividing by 1.8 before subtracting 32.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A child's temperature is 38.5 °C. What is it in °F? Round to the nearest tenth.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 1.8, then add 32: 38.5 °C = 101.3 °F.
mistakes: Adding 32 before multiplying by 1.8.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Infuse 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride over 8 hours by electronic pump. At what rate in mL/hr?
questions.explanation: Volume divided by time in hours gives the pump rate.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: A provider orders 250 mL over 3 hours by electronic pump. At what rate in mL/hr?

steps.explain: Round pump rates to the nearest whole number.

questions.explanation: Volume divided by hours, rounded to a whole number for an electronic pump.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: A provider orders 600 mL over 4 hours by electronic pump. At what rate in mL/hr?
questions.explanation: Volume divided by hours.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: Cefazolin 1 g in 50 mL is to infuse over 30 minutes by electronic pump. At what rate in mL/hr?
questions.formula: mL/hr = (volume mL / time min) x 60 min/hr
questions.explanation: A pump is always set in mL/hr, even for a 30-minute piggyback: 50 mL in half an hour is 100 mL/hr.
mistakes: Setting the pump to 50 mL/hr (that would take a full hour).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Vancomycin 1.25 g in 250 mL is to infuse over 90 minutes by electronic pump. At what rate in mL/hr?
questions.formula: mL/hr = (volume mL / time min) x 60 min/hr

steps.explain: Round pump rates to the nearest whole number.

questions.explanation: 250 mL over 1.5 hours is 166.67 mL/hr, set as 167 mL/hr. The 1.25 g dose does not enter the rate math.
mistakes: Dividing by 90 and stopping (2.8 mL/hr).
Using 1.9 hr instead of 1.5 hr for 90 minutes.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Famotidine 20 mg in 50 mL is to infuse over 15 minutes by electronic pump. At what rate in mL/hr?
questions.formula: mL/hr = (volume mL / time min) x 60 min/hr
questions.explanation: 15 minutes is a quarter hour, so 50 mL x 4 = 200 mL/hr.
mistakes: Using 0.15 hr for 15 minutes (it is 0.25 hr).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Infuse 500 mL over 4 hours by gravity. The drop factor is 15 gtt/mL. How many gtt/min?

steps.explain: Volume over minutes, times drop factor.
Round gravity drip to a whole number.

questions.explanation: Convert hours to minutes first, then apply the drop factor.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: Infuse 1,000 mL over 8 hours by gravity. The drop factor is 10 gtt/mL. How many gtt/min?

steps.explain: Volume over minutes, times drop factor.

questions.explanation: Convert hours to minutes first, then apply the drop factor.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: Infuse 250 mL over 2 hours by gravity. The drop factor is 20 gtt/mL. How many gtt/min?

steps.explain: Volume over minutes, times drop factor.

questions.explanation: Convert hours to minutes first, then apply the drop factor.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: An IV piggyback of 100 mL is to infuse over 30 minutes by gravity. The drop factor is 15 gtt/mL. How many gtt/min?
questions.formula: gtt/min = (volume mL / time min) x drop factor (gtt/mL)
mistakes: Using 0.5 (hours) in the time slot instead of 30 minutes.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: An IV is to run at 75 mL/hr by gravity using microdrip tubing (60 gtt/mL). How many gtt/min?

steps.explain: Convert the hourly rate to per minute.

questions.explanation: With 60 gtt/mL microdrip tubing, gtt/min always equals mL/hr, because the 60s cancel.
mistakes: Multiplying 75 by 60 without dividing by 60 minutes (4,500).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: An IV is ordered at 125 mL/hr. No pump is available, so it will run by gravity with 10 gtt/mL tubing. How many gtt/min?

steps.explain: Convert the hourly rate to per minute.
You cannot count part of a drop: round to a whole number.

questions.explanation: (125 / 60) x 10 = 20.83, so regulate to 21 gtt/min.
mistakes: Rounding down to 20 gtt/min (round normally).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Heparin 1,200 units/hr is ordered. The bag is 25,000 units in 500 mL (50 units/mL). At what rate in mL/hr?

steps.explain: Divide the hourly dose by the concentration.

questions.explanation: Divide the ordered units per hour by the units in each mL.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: The heparin order is increased to 1,400 units/hr. The bag is the same, 25,000 units in 500 mL. At what rate in mL/hr?

steps.explain: Divide the hourly dose by 50 units/mL.

questions.explanation: Divide the ordered units per hour by the units in each mL.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: Dopamine 5 mcg/kg/min is ordered for a client who weighs 154 lb. The bag is 400 mg in 250 mL (1,600 mcg/mL). At what rate in mL/hr? Round to the nearest tenth.

rounding.label: to the nearest tenth
rounding.note: This question asks for the nearest tenth, not a whole number.

questions.formula: 1) kg = lb / 2.2  2) mcg/min = mcg/kg/min x kg  3) mL/hr = (mcg/min x 60) / concentration (mcg/mL)

steps.explain: Round to the nearest tenth as the question asks.

questions.explanation: Convert to kg, then mcg/min, then mL/hr.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: Dopamine 8 mcg/kg/min is ordered for a client who weighs 176 lb. The bag is 400 mg in 250 mL (1,600 mcg/mL). At what rate in mL/hr by electronic pump?
questions.formula: 1) kg = lb / 2.2  2) mcg/min = mcg/kg/min x kg  3) mL/hr = (mcg/min x 60) / concentration (mcg/mL)
questions.explanation: Convert to kg, then mcg/min, then mL/hr.
questions.source: Master Guide, Section 8: High-Yield IV Calculation Formulas

questions.stem: A heparin drip is infusing at 18 mL/hr. The bag is 25,000 units in 250 mL. How many units/hr is the client receiving?

steps.explain: Multiply the rate by the concentration.

questions.explanation: This is a reverse calculation: rate x concentration gives the dose. 18 x 100 = 1,800 units/hr.
mistakes: Using 50 units/mL from the more common 25,000 units/500 mL bag.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Heparin 18 units/kg/hr is ordered for a client who weighs 80 kg. The bag is 25,000 units in 500 mL. At what rate in mL/hr?
questions.formula: 1) units/hr = units/kg/hr x kg  2) mL/hr = units/hr / concentration

steps.explain: Round pump rates to the nearest whole number.

questions.explanation: 18 units/kg/hr x 80 kg = 1,440 units/hr; at 50 units/mL that is 28.8, set as 29 mL/hr.
mistakes: Skipping the weight step and dividing 18 by 50.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Regular insulin is infusing per protocol. The bag is 100 units in 100 mL. The new order is 6.5 units/hr. At what rate in mL/hr? Round to the nearest tenth.

rounding.label: to the nearest tenth
rounding.note: Critical care titrations are set to the tenth; this question asks for the nearest tenth.

steps.explain: Divide the hourly dose by the concentration.

questions.explanation: At 1 unit/mL, units/hr and mL/hr are the same number: 6.5 mL/hr. Only regular insulin is given IV.
mistakes: Rounding to 7 mL/hr when the protocol titrates in tenths.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Norepinephrine 4 mg in 250 mL is infusing at 30 mL/hr. How many mcg/min is the client receiving?
questions.explanation: Reverse calculation: 30 mL/hr x 16 mcg/mL = 480 mcg/hr, divided by 60 = 8 mcg/min.
mistakes: Forgetting to convert mg to mcg (0.008).
Forgetting to divide by 60 (480).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: Dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL is infusing at 15 mL/hr for a client who weighs 80 kg. How many mcg/kg/min is the client receiving?
questions.explanation: Work the forward formula backwards: (15 x 1,600) / 60 / 80 = 5 mcg/kg/min.
mistakes: Leaving out the weight step (400 mcg/min).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is metoprolol tartrate 37.5 mg PO. Available: 25 mg per scored tablet. How many tablets will the nurse give?

steps.work: 37.5 mg / 25 mg x 1 scored tablet = 1.5 tablets
steps.explain: Desired over have, times the quantity the dose comes in.

questions.explanation: Use D/H x Q. 37.5 mg is 1.5 of the 25 mg scored tablets. Only scored, immediate-release tablets may be split.
mistakes: Splitting an extended-release (succinate/XL) tablet. Never split ER or EC tablets.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is amoxicillin oral suspension 500 mg PO. Available: 250 mg per 5 mL. How many mL will the nurse give?

steps.explain: Desired over have, times the quantity the dose comes in.

questions.explanation: Use D/H x Q. 500 mg is twice the 250 mg in each 5 mL, so give 10 mL.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is acetaminophen oral solution 650 mg PO. Available: 160 mg per 5 mL. How many mL will the nurse give?

steps.explain: Desired over have, times the quantity the dose comes in.

questions.explanation: Use D/H x Q. Volumes greater than 1 mL are rounded to the nearest tenth.
mistakes: Rounding to the nearest whole mL. Oral syringes and cups allow measuring tenths.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is levothyroxine 0.15 mg PO. Available: 75 mcg per tablet. How many tablets will the nurse give?

steps.explain: Convert mg to mcg so the order matches the label.
Desired over have, times the quantity the dose comes in.

questions.explanation: Use D/H x Q after converting units. Convert the order to the unit on the label first: 0.15 mg = 150 mcg.
mistakes: Dividing 0.15 by 75 without converting units, which gives a dose 1,000 times too small.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is morphine 3 mg IV push. Available: 4 mg per mL. How many mL will the nurse give?

steps.explain: Desired over have, times the quantity the dose comes in.

questions.explanation: Use D/H x Q. The volume is less than 1 mL, so round to the nearest hundredth and draw it up in a 1 mL syringe.
mistakes: Rounding 0.75 mL to 0.8 mL. Volumes under 1 mL go to the nearest hundredth.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is heparin 5,000 units subcut. Available: 10,000 units per mL. How many mL will the nurse give?

steps.explain: Desired over have, times the quantity the dose comes in.

questions.explanation: Use D/H x Q. Write the answer with a leading zero (0.5 mL) and use a 1 mL syringe.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV push. Available: 2 mg per mL. How many mL will the nurse give?

steps.explain: Desired over have, times the quantity the dose comes in.

questions.explanation: Use D/H x Q. Hydromorphone is a high-alert opioid; small volumes need a 1 mL syringe and an independent double check per facility policy.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM. Ceftriaxone 1 g vial. Label: add 2.1 mL diluent to yield 350 mg/mL. How many mL will the nurse give?
questions.available: Ceftriaxone 1 g vial. Label: add 2.1 mL diluent to yield 350 mg/mL.
questions.formula: Volume = Desired dose / Concentration after reconstitution

steps.explain: Use the concentration printed on the label for 2.1 mL of diluent. The diluent volume itself is not part of the dose math.
Desired dose over the final concentration.

questions.explanation: After reconstitution, use the final concentration on the label (350 mg/mL). The powder adds volume, so the total is more than 2.1 mL.
mistakes: Dividing by the diluent volume (2.1 mL) instead of using the labeled concentration.
Forgetting to label the vial with the date, time, concentration and your initials after mixing.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.available: Cefazolin 1 g vial. Label: add 2.5 mL diluent to yield 330 mg/mL.
questions.formula: Volume = Desired dose / Concentration after reconstitution

steps.explain: Use the concentration printed on the label for 2.5 mL of diluent. The diluent volume itself is not part of the dose math.
Desired dose over the final concentration.

questions.explanation: After reconstitution, use the final concentration on the label (330 mg/mL).

questions.available: Ampicillin 500 mg vial. Label: add 1.8 mL diluent to yield 250 mg/mL.
questions.formula: Volume = Desired dose / Concentration after reconstitution

Desired dose over the final concentration.

questions.stem: The order is methylprednisolone sodium succinate 40 mg IV push. Methylprednisolone sodium succinate 125 mg vial. Label: add 2 mL diluent to yield 62.5 mg/mL. How many mL will the nurse give?
questions.order: Methylprednisolone sodium succinate 40 mg IV push
questions.available: Methylprednisolone sodium succinate 125 mg vial. Label: add 2 mL diluent to yield 62.5 mg/mL.
questions.formula: Volume = Desired dose / Concentration after reconstitution

steps.explain: Use the concentration printed on the label for 2 mL of diluent. The diluent volume itself is not part of the dose math.
Desired dose over the final concentration.

questions.explanation: After reconstitution, use the final concentration on the label (62.5 mg/mL). The volume is less than 1 mL, so round to the nearest hundredth.
mistakes: Dividing by the diluent volume (2 mL) instead of using the labeled concentration.
Forgetting to label the vial with the date, time, concentration and your initials after mixing.

questions.stem: A child weighing 44 lb has an order for acetaminophen 15 mg/kg/dose PO every 6 hours as needed for fever. Available: 160 mg per 5 mL. How many mL will the nurse give per dose?
questions.order: Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg/dose PO every 6 hours as needed for fever
questions.formula: 1) kg = lb / 2.2  2) mg = mg/kg x kg  3) mL = mg / concentration

steps.explain: Convert to kg and round to the nearest tenth before calculating the dose.

questions.explanation: Convert to kg, find the mg dose, then convert to mL. Do not exceed 5 doses in 24 hours.
mistakes: Using the weight in pounds (44 x 15 = 660 mg), which more than doubles the dose.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.order: Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg/dose PO every 6 hours as needed for fever
questions.formula: 1) kg = lb / 2.2  2) mg = mg/kg x kg  3) mL = mg / concentration

steps.explain: Convert to kg and round to the nearest tenth before calculating the dose.

questions.explanation: Convert to kg, find the mg dose, then convert to mL.

questions.stem: An adult weighing 187 lb has an order for enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcut every 12 hours. Available: prefilled syringe 100 mg/mL. How many mL will the nurse give?
questions.formula: 1) kg = lb / 2.2  2) mg = 1 mg/kg x kg  3) mL = mg / 100 mg/mL

steps.explain: Convert to kg and round to the nearest tenth.
Volume under 1 mL: round to the nearest hundredth.

questions.explanation: Convert to kg, find the mg dose, then the volume. Expel excess from the prefilled syringe before giving; do not expel the air bubble.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A child weighing 22 lb is prescribed amoxicillin. The safe range is 25-50 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours. What is the maximum safe single dose in mg?
questions.available: Safe range: 25-50 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours
questions.formula: Max single dose = (max mg/kg/day x kg) / doses per day

steps.explain: Every 12 hours is 2 doses per day.

questions.explanation: Find the maximum daily dose, then divide by the number of doses per day (q12h = 2).
mistakes: Stopping at the daily dose (500 mg) and giving it as a single dose.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A child weighing 22 lb has an order for amoxicillin 300 mg PO every 12 hours. The safe range is 25-50 mg/kg/day. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose; it is within the safe range.
Hold the dose and contact the provider; the order exceeds the safe range.
Hold the dose and contact the provider; the order is below the therapeutic range.
Give half the dose and document the change.

questions.explanation: 10 kg x 25-50 mg/kg/day = 250-500 mg/day. The order is 300 mg x 2 = 600 mg/day, which is above the 500 mg/day maximum, so it is an overdose. Hold it and clarify with the provider.

why.A: 600 mg/day is above the 500 mg/day maximum.
why.C: The order is above the range, not below 250 mg/day.
why.D: Nurses do not change a dose without a new order.

questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A child weighing 37.4 lb is prescribed cephalexin. The safe range is 25-50 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours. What is the maximum safe daily dose in mg?
questions.available: Safe range: 25-50 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours
questions.formula: Max daily dose = max mg/kg/day x kg
questions.explanation: Multiply the top of the range by the weight in kg.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A child weighing 37.4 lb has an order for cephalexin 75 mg PO every 6 hours. The safe range is 25-50 mg/kg/day. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The dose is safe and therapeutic; give it.
The dose is an overdose; hold it and contact the provider.
The dose is below the therapeutic range; contact the provider before giving it.
The dose is safe because each single dose is small.

questions.explanation: 17 kg x 25-50 mg/kg/day = 425-850 mg/day. The order is 75 mg x 4 = 300 mg/day, below the 425 mg/day minimum. An underdose may not treat the infection, so clarify with the provider.

why.A: 300 mg/day is below the 425 mg/day minimum.
why.B: The order is below the range, not above 850 mg/day.
why.D: Safety is judged on the daily total against the mg/kg/day range, not on how small one dose looks.

steps.explain: Every 6 hours is 4 doses per day.

questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A client's fingerstick glucose before lunch is 245 mg/dL. Using the correction scale, how many units of insulin lispro will the nurse give?
questions.order: Insulin lispro subcut per correction scale before meals
questions.available: Correction scale (insulin lispro): 150-199 mg/dL = 2 units; 200-249 = 4 units; 250-299 = 6 units; 300-349 = 8 units; 350 or higher = call the provider. Below 150 = no correction.
questions.formula: Find the range that contains the glucose value; give the units for that range.

steps.explain: Match the reading to its range.
Read the dose for that range.

questions.explanation: Match the glucose reading to the correct range on the scale. 245 is in the 200-249 range.
mistakes: Reading the next range up because 245 is close to 250.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A client has an order for insulin lispro 6 units subcut with meals plus correction per scale. The glucose before dinner is 312 mg/dL and the client is about to eat. What is the total dose of insulin lispro?
questions.patient: Fingerstick glucose 312 mg/dL; meal tray at bedside
questions.order: Insulin lispro 6 units subcut with meals, plus correction scale
questions.available: Correction scale (insulin lispro): 150-199 mg/dL = 2 units; 200-249 = 4 units; 250-299 = 6 units; 300-349 = 8 units; 350 or higher = call the provider. Below 150 = no correction.
questions.formula: Total = scheduled mealtime dose + correction dose

steps.explain: Add it to the scheduled mealtime dose; both are the same rapid-acting insulin.

questions.explanation: When the scheduled and correction doses are the same insulin, add them and give one injection.
mistakes: Giving only the correction dose and leaving out the scheduled mealtime dose.
Giving rapid-acting insulin when the meal is not available.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is insulin glargine 18 units subcut at bedtime. The vial is U-100 (100 units/mL). How many mL is this dose?
questions.order: Insulin glargine 18 units subcut at bedtime

steps.explain: Divide the dose by the concentration.

questions.explanation: U-100 insulin has 100 units in each mL. In practice, draw insulin up in units with a U-100 insulin syringe; the mL value shows how small the volume is.
mistakes: Using a tuberculin (mL) syringe instead of an insulin syringe.
Mixing insulin glargine with any other insulin.
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: The order is regular insulin U-500 150 units subcut before breakfast. The vial is U-500 (500 units/mL). How many mL is this dose?
questions.order: Regular insulin U-500 150 units subcut before breakfast

steps.explain: Divide the dose by the concentration.

questions.explanation: U-500 is five times as concentrated as U-100. Measure it only with a U-500 syringe or the U-500 pen, which are marked in units of U-500, never with a U-100 syringe.
mistakes: Drawing 150 units in a U-100 syringe, which gives 750 units (five times the dose).
questions.source: NursePrepHub original (AI-drafted via /medmath); standard dimensional analysis. Needs nurse-educator review.

questions.stem: A client's fingerstick glucose before breakfast is 368 mg/dL. Using the correction scale, what should the nurse do?
questions.order: Insulin lispro subcut per correction scale before meals
questions.available: Correction scale (insulin lispro): 150-199 mg/dL = 2 units; 200-249 = 4 units; 250-299 = 6 units; 300-349 = 8 units; 350 or higher = call the provider. Below 150 = no correction.

options.text: Give 8 units, the highest dose on the scale.
Contact the provider for orders, as the scale directs.
